Description: A limestone sarcophagus of Ahiram, a Phoenician king of Byblos (about 1000 BC), discovered in 1923 by Pierre Montet in Tomb V of the royal necropolis at Byblos, revealed by a landslide. Its 38-word Phoenician inscription (KAI 1), commissioned by his son Ittobaal, curses anyone who disturbs the coffin. It is now in the National Museum of Beirut.
Interpretations: The inscription is the earliest known example of the fully developed Phoenician alphabet (19 of 22 letters present), the script family from which Greek, Latin, Cyrillic, Hebrew, and Arabic alphabets descend. Caution: Ahiram is not attested in any other ancient source, and a suggested connection to the biblical King Hiram is only a scholarly suggestion; Ahiram must not be identified as Hiram, and no Hiram passage is linked here.
AlternativeNames: Ahirom Sarcophagus; Sarcophagus of King Ahiram
BiblicalSignificance: It preserves the earliest fully developed Phoenician alphabet, the writing system from which the Hebrew script of the Old Testament descends.
